transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-23
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park, Miguel Soto, Priya Mehta (Redwood) — Aisha Khan, Tom Reynolds, Derek Liu, Maya Ortiz (Oakbridge)

--- Optional auto-summary: quick notes by recorder: Oakbridge leaning toward Hosted for initial pilot but wants deterministic p95 for chat use case. Key concerns: data residency, KMS integration, and predictable p95 under token bursts.

Topics:
- p95 latency targets (chat & streaming)
- peak concurrency & token/sec burst profiles
- hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
- benchmarking plan and fallbacks
- security controls (KMS, SSO, audit logs)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for jumping on, can we do quick intros and then jump into the hosting questions?
[00:07] Aisha (Oakbridge): yeah hi I'm Aisha, head of ML at Oakbridge. We own the behavioral models and production chat. Tom's platform, Derek is SRE. Maya does security.
[00:15] Miguel (Redwood SE): hi all, Miguel here. I'll run through how we measure p95 and where dedicated/private give different guarantees.
[00:22] Tom (Oakbridge): quick note, we have two main flows: live chat (mostly short prompts, median 20-40 tokens, target p95 low) and analytics path (longer prompts, batch, 300-1k tokens, throughput matters).
[00:34] Lena: great, and what's the p95 target you're expecting for chat?
[00:38] Aisha: ideally p95 under 300ms for the live responses, with streaming enabled. If it's a hair over, like 350, that's okay but we need consistency.
[00:46] Derek: also need to understand concurrency — we see spikes to 120 concurrent chats during earnings, sustained 30-50 normally.
[00:54] Miguel: ok that's helpful. For Hosted, our typical profiles show p95 in 200-350ms for small-chat on our fast verified models under moderate load, but during token bursts it can slip if autoscale isn't warmed.
[01:10] Maya: big question for us is KMS — can we bring our own key for encrypted logs and model request traces? Also audit log retention.
[01:18] Priya (Redwood CSM): yes we support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated; Hosted has a managed KMS option and we can negotiate Bring-Your-Own-Key in enterprise tier. We'll include the doc.
[01:27] Aisha: perfect — regarding throughput for our analytics pipeline, we measure in tokens/sec. We need sustained 400-600 tok/sec for a batch ingestion job without latency tail spikes.
[01:36] Miguel: that's feasible on Dedicated — with optimized batching and quantized model variants you can hit that class of throughput on a small pool. Hosted can too but with less guarantee on sustained window lengths unless you reserve capacity.
[01:52] Tom: when you say 'quantized variant' — is inference quality materially different? We care about hallucination rates.
[01:59] Miguel: good question. For many tasks, 4-bit quantized variants are within tolerable quality delta; for safety-sensitive content we recommend FP16 or int8 hybrid. We can run a quality regression on your prompt set to show delta.
[02:16] [crosstalk] Aisha: ok, so we want both latency and quality metrics from your tests.
[02:21] Miguel: yes we'll run token/sec benchmarks plus a quality compare, and include p95 distributions.
[02:27] [03:00] Lena: can you outline what success looks like for you for the pilot?
[03:05] Aisha: pilot should validate three things: 1) p95 for chat under 300-350ms at our expected concurrency, 2) sustained throughput 400-600 tok/sec on analytics jobs for 1 hour windows, 3) security posture meets our KMS and audit needs.
[03:20] Tom: and we need a fallback policy if capacity is constrained — e.g., degrade to a smaller model or fall back to shorter context.
[03:28] Miguel: our routing policies support automated fallback to cheaper/compatible variants, region failover, and queued responses. We'll demo that in the deep-dive.
[03:38] Derek: curious about steady-state cold starts, do you have numbers for cold KV-cache misses? We saw big tail when cache was cold.
[03:45] Miguel: cold KV-cache misses can add 50-150ms depending on model and seq len. We mitigate with warm pools and prefix caching; Dedicated gives you more control of the cache warm-up policy.
[03:58] Maya: any SOC2 / ISO attestation for Hosted? Our auditors care.
[04:03] Priya: Hosted is SOC 2 Type II certified and we have ISO docs; Private deployment can live behind your control plane if required. We'll share our compliance pack.
[04:14] [04:30] Miguel: for benchmarking plan — we'd like a sample corpus from you: 2000 chat samples and 400 batch prompts representative of analytics. We'll run:
- short-chat p95 distributions under synthetic concurrency profiles (10, 50, 120)
- token/sec sustained runs (1 hour windows) for analytics pipeline
- streaming token-per-second real-time throughput test with incremental ramp to peak

[04:55] Tom: ramp to peak is important — we have holiday peak patterns so we'd want 10x baseline for 5-10 minutes.
[05:03] Miguel: noted; we'll include a burst-surge test with 5-10 minute windows.
[05:09] Aisha: what's your failure mode during oversubscription? If we hit capacity, do requests queue, fail, or get routed?
[05:16] Lena: by policy we can queue with backpressure, route to a lower-cost variant, or fallback to cached response. We work with customers to choose policy per route.
[05:25] Derek: and what about per-token cost delta when using streaming vs batched completions?
[05:31] Miguel: streaming doesn't change token cost, but batching for analytics reduces tokens/sec cost because of amortized overhead. We can show expected unit economics in the cost model.
[05:42] [06:00] Miguel: quick aside — we've seen that p95 for streaming is sensitive to first-token latency; to meet p95 < 300ms we need headroom for the first token path and consistent kernel scheduling.
[06:12] Aisha: do you support custom kernel selection or tuning for private deployments?
[06:17] Miguel: yes Private gives you the most control — we can onboard custom kernel optimizations and pick quantization kernels per workload. For Hosted, we manage kernel selection but expose profiles.
[06:29] Tom: can you run a simple rough calc: if we want p95 under 300ms at 120 concurrency, what kind of reserved pool do we need?
[06:36] Miguel: rough back-of-envelope: for small-chat median 30 tokens, assuming 10ms token generation per token on optimized kernels — that's 300ms for 30 tokens so you need pipelined streaming to get first token faster. In practice a dedicated r3-pool of 4 GPUs (example) can cover 100-150 concurrent small-chat at p95 under 300ms depending on model. We'll run exact numbers with your prompt set.
[07:01] [07:30] Aisha: can we also test a smaller model fallback in those runs? E.g., degrade to a 2B variant if the main model is overloaded.
[07:38] Miguel: absolutely — our routing layer can automate an A/B style fallback. We'll include that in the benchmark runs.
[07:46] Lena: let's talk timeline — we're proposing a 3-month pilot, first two weeks integration and sample data exchange, then a 30-day testing window for benchmarks, then an operational review. Sound OK?
[07:58] Tom: that's reasonable. We'll need procurement loops for Dedicated though. Hosted pilot easier to start.
[08:04] Maya: procurement will want an example contract and data processing addendum; send those.
[08:09] Lena: will do.
[08:13] [08:30] Miguel: any stateful conversation concerns? If you use long context and KV caches across interactions, the memory footprint and cache evictions can influence p95. We recommend explicit session affinity if that matters.
[08:44] Derek: we do session affinity for personalization and we can't tolerate crossing users. So per-session KV cache and encrypted state is important.
[08:52] Miguel: Private or Dedicated both support per-session affinity and encrypted caches; Hosted has session isolation as well but for the most stringent regulatory needs Private is preferred.
[09:03] Aisha: what about multi-region failover? We need EU data residency and reliable failover to US if EU region degrades.
[09:12] Miguel: routing policies can prefer EU for residency and failover to US with redaction rules. We'll document the approach.
[09:20] [09:45] Tom: any vendor lock-in concerns? If we start with Hosted and later move to Private, how hard is migration?
[09:53] Priya: the API and configs are identical across modes — we build migration tooling for model pins and routing. Moving from Hosted to Dedicated/Private is largely a deployment change with some network config.
[10:06] Aisha: okay good.
[10:10] [10:30] Miguel: for benchmarks we'll produce: p95 histograms, token/sec time series, quality regression report on your labels, and a cost per token breakdown.
[10:22] Derek: can you include memory usage and GPU util traces? Our SREs will want that.
[10:27] Miguel: yes, we'll share per-host GPU util and kernel scheduling traces — some of those are obfuscated for Hosted but full traces available for Dedicated/Private.
[10:38] [11:00] Aisha: one last question — do you support pre-warmed pools and standby capacity for predictable p95?
[11:06] Miguel: yes, dedicated reserved capacity can be pre-warmed and we offer a standby burst fund for Hosted to reduce cold starts.
[11:12] Lena: ok let's summarize action items and next steps.
[11:17] Lena: Miguel will run the 72-hour microbenchmark using their sample prompts and include fallbacks. Lena will send proposal and pricing. Priya will send compliance pack. Oakbridge will send sample corpus and confirm procurement timeline.
[11:31] Aisha: thanks all — excited to see the numbers.
[11:34] Tom: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription fidelity: occasional words like 'KV cache' transcribed as 'K-V cash', some speaker attribution generic in two short places where crosstalk happened. Overall medium quality with filler words and run-ons preserved.
